title: Low-Multiplicity Jets as Probes of GeV-Scale Light-Quark-Coupled Particles
summary: We propose a search at the LHC for GeV-scale particles coupling predominantly to light quarks based on low-multiplicity jets. The search targets production in association with a hard photon and uses the feature that a light gauge-singlet can only decay into a small number of hadronic channels, yielding jets with anomalously low charged-track multiplicity and mass compared to QCD jets at the same transverse momentum. We determine the sensitivity to scalar and pseudoscalar couplings to up-quarks, and suggest a data-driven estimate that reduces the sensitivity to jet modeling uncertainties. This search extends the reach to hadronically-coupled particles into a previously inaccessible regime.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a new search strategy at the LHC for GeV-scale particles that couple to light quarks, focusing on low-multiplicity jets associated with hard photons.
AI.motivation: To explore the production and decay of light gauge-singlet particles that manifest as low multiplicity jets, previously unexplored in hadronic coupling regimes.
AI.method: The search utilizes low-multiplicity jets produced alongside hard photons, analyzing jets with characteristics differing from typical QCD jets, and incorporates a data-driven approach to account for jet modeling uncertainties.
AI.result: The study quantitatively assesses the sensitivity to scalar and pseudoscalar couplings to up-quarks, revealing the ability to probe a previously inaccessible parameter space for hadronically-coupled particles.
AI.conclusion: This research opens new avenues for investigating light quark-coupled particles at the LHC, enhancing the sensitivity of searches in a previously unexplored energy regime.

title: Self-Interaction and Galactic Magnetic Field Bounds on Millicharged Magnetic Monopole Dark Matter
summary: A dark matter sector composed of magnetic monopoles of a dark U(1) symmetry having a small kinetic mixing with the Standard Model photon has a rich and interesting phenomenology. The model in itself is also of theoretical interest. Based on the temperature of the dark sector and scale of spontaneous symmetry breaking for this U(1), three phenomenologically distinct cases for this model of dark matter are discussed. In all cases, constraints on dark matter self-interactions are translated into constraints on the model parameters. As the magnetic monopoles acquire a small visible magnetic charge, the survival of galactic magnetic fields, known as the Parker effect, places further constraints on the mixing between the dark and visible sectors.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a model of dark matter involving magnetic monopoles with small kinetic mixing with Standard Model photons, exploring different cases based on temperature and symmetry breaking with significant phenomenological implications.
AI.motivation: To explore the theoretical interest and phenomenological consequences of a dark matter sector made of magnetic monopoles connected to a dark U(1) symmetry.
AI.method: The paper discusses three distinct phenomenological scenarios based on the dark sector's temperature and the spontaneous symmetry breaking scale, and relates dark matter self-interaction constraints to model parameters.
AI.result: The study establishes that the magnetic monopoles interacting with Standard Model photons through kinetic mixing impose significant constraints from dark matter self-interactions and the survival of galactic magnetic fields.
AI.conclusion: The model provides an intriguing framework for understanding dark matter, highlighting the interplay between dark and visible sectors and the implications for galactic magnetic field survival.

title: A First Account of the Impact of Ion Electromagnetic Dissociation on Event Exclusivity in Ultraperipheral LHC Collisions
summary: In this Letter we explore the modelling of hadron production in electromagnetic ion dissociation (EMD) processes in high-energy ultraperipheral collisions at LHC energies. Since EMD can accompany exclusive particle production in these interactions, we demonstrate that the resulting hadrons can break the exclusivity vetos typically imposed by experiments. As two representative examples, we calculate the impact on existing LHC measurements of exclusive muon pair production ($γγ\toμμ$) and exclusive coherent $J/ψ$ production. We demonstrate that accounting for this effect resolves long-standing tensions between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper examines hadron production in electromagnetic ion dissociation during high-energy ultraperipheral collisions, showing its significance in exclusive particle production processes at the LHC and resolving discrepancies between theory and experiments.
AI.motivation: To address the oversight of hadron production in electromagnetic ion dissociation processes that accompany exclusive particle production in high-energy collisions.
AI.method: The authors calculate the influence of hadron production on LHC measurements of exclusive muon pair production and exclusive J/ψ production, considering how this alters the expected outcomes.
AI.result: Incorporating hadron production modifies the understanding of exclusive processes, leading to reconciliations of existing theoretical predictions and experimental data.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights the importance of hadron production in EMD processes, suggesting that it can resolve discrepancies previously observed in LHC experimental results.

title: Ultra-High-Energy Tau Neutrinos as Probes of Lorentz Invariance
summary: Neutrino telescopes have detected astrophysical neutrinos with energies up to ${O}(100)$ PeV. Several current and proposed experiments aim to observe neutrinos at even higher energies, with the goal of detecting cosmogenic neutrinos. This increase in neutrino energy makes tests of Lorentz invariance violation (LIV) particularly appealing, since the effects of higher-dimension LIV operators on neutrino propagation grow rapidly with energy. In this work, we investigate the potential of the upcoming experiments GRAND and POEMMA to probe LIV in the neutrino sector through the detection of ultra-high-energy tau neutrinos. We generate the cosmogenic neutrino flux using SimProp and interface it with a calculation of neutrino flavor transition probabilities in the presence of LIV effects. Deviations from standard flavor transition probabilities manifest as changes in the expected tau neutrino event rates at GRAND and POEMMA. We first consider the case with a single nonzero LIV operator of various dimensions, and find that the projected sensitivities exceed existing limits from lower-energy probes by orders of magnitude. We then explore scenarios with multiple nonzero LIV parameters and show that their interplay can significantly modify the sensitivities compared to the single-parameter case. Overall, we find that upcoming observations of ultra-high-energy tau neutrinos will place some of the most stringent constraints on LIV.

AI.tldr: This study assesses how upcoming neutrino telescopes GRAND and POEMMA can test Lorentz invariance violation (LIV) by measuring ultra-high-energy tau neutrinos, revealing significantly enhanced sensitivity compared to previous experiments.
AI.motivation: To explore the potential of upcoming experiments to detect LIV in neutrino propagation through ultra-high-energy tau neutrinos, as higher energies amplify the effects of LIV.
AI.method: Use SimProp to generate cosmogenic neutrino flux and compute neutrino flavor transition probabilities influenced by LIV effects, analyzing event rates at GRAND and POEMMA.
AI.result: Projected sensitivities to LIV parameters surpass existing limits from lower-energy observations by orders of magnitude and consider interactions between multiple LIV parameters.
AI.conclusion: Future detections of ultra-high-energy tau neutrinos will offer some of the most rigorous constraints on Lorentz invariance violation.

title: Neural posterior estimation of the neutrino direction in IceCube using transformer-encoded normalizing flows on the sphere
summary: IceCube is a cubic-kilometer-scale neutrino detector located at the geographic South Pole. A precise directional reconstruction of IceCube neutrinos is vital for associations with astronomical objects. In this context, we discuss neural posterior estimation of the neutrino direction via a transformer encoder that maps to a normalizing flow on the 2-sphere. It achieves a new state-of-the-art angular resolution for the two main event morphologies in IceCube - tracks and showers - while being significantly faster than traditional B-spline-based likelihood reconstructions. All-sky scans can be performed within seconds rather than hours, and take constant computation time, regardless of whether the posterior extent is arc-minutes or spans the whole sky. We utilize a combination of $C^2$-smooth rational-quadratic splines, scale transformations and rotations to define a novel spherical normalizing-flow distribution whose parameters are predicted as a whole as the output of the transformer encoder. We test several structural choices diverting from the vanilla transformer architecture. In particular, we find dual residual streams, nonlinear QKV projection and a separate class token with its own cross-attention processing to boost test-time performance. The angular resolution for both showers and tracks improves substantially over the whole trained energy range from 100 GeV to 100 PeV. At 100 TeV deposited energy, for example, the median angular resolution improves by a factor of $1.3$ for throughgoing tracks, by a factor of $1.7$ for showers and by a factor of $2.5$ for starting tracks compared to state-of-the art likelihood reconstructions based on B-splines. While previous machine-learning (ML) efforts have managed to obtain competitive shower resolutions, this is the first time an ML-based method outperforms likelihood-based muon reconstructions above 100 GeV.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a neural network approach using a transformer encoder for improving the directional reconstruction of neutrinos in the IceCube detector, achieving superior angular resolution and faster computation compared to traditional methods.
AI.motivation: Precise directional reconstruction of neutrinos is crucial for correlating them with astronomical objects, necessitating improved methods for analysis.
AI.method: Utilizes a transformer encoder in conjunction with a normalizing flow on the 2-sphere, employing novel structural choices like dual residual streams and nonlinear projections to enhance performance.
AI.result: Achieves new state-of-the-art angular resolution for both tracks and showers in IceCube, with significant improvement factors over previous likelihood-based methods, especially at high energies.
AI.conclusion: This ML-based technique sets a new benchmark for neutrino direction reconstruction, outperforming traditional methods and facilitating faster all-sky scans.

title: Quantum Integrated High-Performance Computing: Foundations, Architectural Elements and Future Directions
summary: High-performance computing (HPC) has evolved over decades through multiple architectural transitions, from vector supercomputers to massively parallel CPU clusters and GPU-accelerated systems, continuously expanding the frontier of scientific discovery. With the emergence of quantum processing units (QPUs) as practical computational accelerators, a new opportunity arises to further extend this trajectory by integrating quantum and classical computing paradigms. This paper presents Quantum Integrated High-Performance Computing (QHPC), a visionary architectural framework that unifies CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and QPUs as first-class heterogeneous resources. We propose a layered system design comprising unified resource management, quantum-aware scheduling, hybrid workflow orchestration, middleware and programming abstraction, interconnect technologies, and a tiered execution model enabling seamless workload partitioning across classical and quantum backends. A central aspect of our vision is a strong user requests abstraction layer that exposes heterogeneous resources through a unified job submission interface, similar in spirit to existing schedulers such as Slurm, allowing users to describe workloads in a consistent template independent of underlying compute type or location. Drawing insights from prior accelerator integration eras, we outline how QHPC can support emerging workloads in quantum chemistry, materials discovery, combinatorial optimization, and climate modeling. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in building scalable, reliable, and programmable quantum-classical infrastructures that seamlessly connect global users to heterogeneous compute resources for future quantum-classical HPC ecosystems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Quantum Integrated High-Performance Computing (QHPC), a framework that combines quantum and classical computing resources to enhance computational capabilities for scientific discovery.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to explore the integration of quantum processing units (QPUs) with existing computing paradigms to expand HPC's potential in scientific research.
AI.method: QHPC proposes a layered system design featuring unified resource management, quantum-aware scheduling, middleware, and a unified job submission interface to streamline workloads across different compute architectures.
AI.result: The QHPC framework is designed to efficiently handle emerging workloads in fields like quantum chemistry and climate modeling through a hybrid orchestration of classical and quantum resources.
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies challenges in creating scalable quantum-classical infrastructures, emphasizing the need for reliable connections between diverse computing resources in future HPC ecosystems.

title: Stability of Charge Collection Efficiency and Time Resolution in a Novel Ultra-fast Graphene-Optimized Silicon Carbide Detector Under X-ray Irradiation
summary: A graphene-optimized silicon carbide PIN detector was fabricated and its radiation tolerance under X-ray irradiation of 160 keV was evaluated. Its electrical properties, charge collection performance and time resolution of beta-particles (90Sr) are reported. After 1 MGy irradiation, the detector maintains an ultralow leakage current of approximately 2.2e-10 A @ 300 V and the C-V characteristics are basically consistent with full depletion at 120V. The time resolution of the graphene-optimized silicon carbide detector is 58.0 ps. The time resolution is comparable to that of state-of-the-art 4H-SiC low-gain avalanche detectors (LGADs). The G/RE 4H-SiC PIN detector exhibits outstanding time resolution performance. Compared with the time resolution of the RE 4H-SiC PIN detector, the time resolution of the G/RE 4H-SiC PIN detector has decreased by 39.6%. This demonstrates the significance of the graphene electrode design. The graphene detector exhibits a charge collection efficiency (CCE) of 99.24% after X-ray irradiation, along with excellent stability. The graphene-optimized silicon carbide detector maintains good timing resolution: 58.0ps before and 64.0ps after X-ray irradiation. Experimental results indicate that the CCE and time resolution performance exhibit good stability before and after irradiation. These results demonstrate stable performance under extreme X-ray exposure, highlighting the detectors potential for radiation-hard applications in high-energy physics, space missions, and nuclear reactor monitoring.

AI.tldr: The graphene-optimized SiC PIN detector demonstrates excellent radiation tolerance and stability under high-energy X-ray exposure, with impressive time resolution and charge collection performance.
AI.motivation: To develop a radiation-tolerant detector for applications in high-energy physics, space missions, and nuclear reactor monitoring, utilizing graphene in the design.
AI.method: Fabrication and evaluation of a graphene-optimized silicon carbide PIN detector under 160 keV X-ray irradiation, measuring electrical properties, charge collection efficiency, and time resolution.
AI.result: After 1 MGy irradiation, the detector showed low leakage current, good C-V characteristics, time resolution of 58.0 ps, and a charge collection efficiency of 99.24%, with stability before and after irradiation.
AI.conclusion: The graphene electrode design significantly enhances the performance of the SiC detector, making it suitable for extreme radiation environments.

title: The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) Antarctic Balloon Payload
comment: 16 pages, 12 figures, submitted to NIM A
summary: The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) is an Antarctic stratospheric balloon mission designed to provide unmatched sensitivity to low-energy (<0.25 GeV/n) cosmic-ray antiprotons, antideuterons, and antihelium nuclei as signatures of dark matter. The distinctive GAPS particle identification technique relies on measuring the energy loss along the track of an incoming antinucleus as it slows down and is captured into an exotic atom, and then detecting the de-excitation X-rays and the nuclear annihilation products. This measurement is realized using a Tracker composed of more than 1000 custom silicon strip detectors and a plastic scintillator time-of-flight (TOF) system instrumenting more than 40m$^2$. Together, these subsystems provide the velocity and energy resolution, stopping power, particle tracking, and X-ray identification necessary to distinguish rare antinucleus signals from the abundant positive-nucleus backgrounds, all within the constraints of a high-altitude mission. A multi-loop capillary heat pipe system has been developed to maintain the tracker operating temperature with significant mass and power savings over a conventional pump-based system. The first GAPS science payload flew for 25 days during the 2025/26 NASA Antarctic balloon campaign. We detail the design, integration, and commissioning of the payload prior to flight.

AI.tldr: The GAPS mission aims to detect low-energy cosmic-ray antinuclei as potential dark matter signatures using advanced particle identification techniques and a specialized tracker system.
AI.motivation: To improve sensitivity to low-energy cosmic-ray antinuclei for dark matter research.
AI.method: Employing a Tracker with custom silicon strip detectors and a scintillator TOF system to measure energy loss and particle identification while utilizing a heat pipe system for optimal temperature control.
AI.result: Successfully designed, integrated, and commissioned the GAPS payload for its inaugural flight.
AI.conclusion: GAPS represents a significant advancement in detecting cosmic-ray antinuclei, intending to contribute to dark matter investigations.

title: Quasi-Periodic Microstructures in Pulsar Emission: Automated Detection and Archival Survey
summary: The study of quasi-period microstructures in pulsars offers valuable insights into the underlying emission mechanism. However, identifying these features through manual inspection of the intensity time series, often containing thousands to millions of pulses, is both laborious and time-consuming. To address this challenge, we have developed a Python-based software, Quasi-periodic MIcrostructure Search Tool (QMIST), to automate the search for quasi-periodic microstructures in radio pulsar time-series data. We provide a detailed description of the algorithms used in QMIST, demonstrate its efficacy using data on pulsars known to exhibit microstructures, and discuss potential future improvements. Using QMIST, we have performed a multi-epoch survey of quasi-periodic microstructures in a sample of 27 pulsars, using observations from the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope and the Green Bank Telescope, as well as the archival data from the Parkes telescope. In addition to recovering previously reported microstructures from several pulsars, we report, for the first time, detection of quasi-periodic microstructures in three pulsars, B1451-68, B1706-16 and B1845-19. We also estimate the typical period of microstructures in another pulsar, B0540+23, that was known to exhibit microstructures earlier but the periodicity was unknown. Using the periodicity measurements from our survey, and earlier such measurements from the literature, we confirm the near linear relationship between the microstructure periodicity and the rotation period of pulsars, and discuss our results in the context of the emission mechanism of microstructures.

AI.tldr: The study introduces QMIST, an automated tool for identifying quasi-periodic microstructures in pulsar data, successfully detects new microstructures in multiple pulsars, and confirms relationships between microstructure periodicity and pulsar rotation periods.
AI.motivation: Identifying quasi-period microstructures in pulsars is labor-intensive and time-consuming, necessitating an automated solution to enhance efficiency and accuracy.
AI.method: Development of the Quasi-periodic MIcrostructure Search Tool (QMIST) for automating the search in radio pulsar time-series data, validated on a multi-epoch survey of 27 pulsars using multiple telescope data.
AI.result: Revealed new detections of quasi-periodic microstructures in three pulsars and estimated periodicity in another known pulsar, confirming the relationship between microstructure periodicity and pulsar rotation periods.
AI.conclusion: The findings enhance understanding of pulsar emission mechanisms and suggest further exploration of microstructure characteristics.

title: Sub-GeV dark matter from cosmic ray bremsstrahlung in the atmosphere
summary: We explore the sensitivity of neutrino observatories and direct dark matter detection experiments to boosted sub-GeV dark matter produced by inelastic cosmic ray collisions in the atmosphere. We revisit earlier approaches and extend the sensitivity to higher mass by modeling the proton bremsstrahlung production mode via initial state radiation. For vector-mediated dark matter models, the peak of the cosmic ray flux allows for enhanced DM production for mediator masses near the $ρ/ω$ resonances. We determine and compare the ensuing sensitivity of direct detection experiments LZ and PandaX-4T and the neutrino detectors Borexino and Super-K.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the ability of neutrino observatories and dark matter detection experiments to detect boosted light dark matter produced by cosmic ray interactions, extending sensitivity to higher masses using new modeling techniques.
AI.motivation: To understand how neutrino observatories and direct detection experiments can detect sub-GeV dark matter generated by cosmic ray collisions, especially at higher masses.
AI.method: The authors model the proton bremsstrahlung production mode through initial state radiation and analyze the impact of cosmic ray flux peaks on dark matter production, particularly focusing on vector-mediated models near the $ρ/ω$ resonances.
AI.result: The study evaluates and compares the sensitivities of various detection experiments, specifically LZ, PandaX-4T, Borexino, and Super-K, to the boosted dark matter signals.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight enhanced sensitivity for detecting certain dark matter models at specific mediator masses, suggesting improved detection strategies for such scenarios.

title: Prospects for measuring exclusive diffractive $η,η'$ at the LHC
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, Proceedings 53rd International Symposium on Multiparticle Dynamics (ISMD 2025), 21.-26. Sept. 2025, Corfu, Greece
summary:
Central exclusive diffractive production in proton-proton collisions
  at hadron colliders is characterised by hadronic activity at or close to
  midrapidity, and by the two forward scattered protons, or their remnants.
  In such events, no particles are produced between the midrapidity system
  and the forward beam particles. These events can hence be identified with
  appropriately placed detectors for measuring the forward scattered protons,
  or their remnants, and a detector system covering the midrapidity range.
  At the energies of the LHC, central diffractive production in proton-proton
  collisions is dominated by pomeron-pomeron fusion. The description of the
  pomeron within the Regge approach is summarized, and the feasibility of
  identifying pseudoscalar mesons $η,η'$ in pomeron-pomeron fusion
  is studied for determining the spin structure of the pomeron.

AI.tldr: The paper discusses central exclusive diffractive production in proton-proton collisions at the LHC, focusing on the detection of events characterized by midrapidity hadronic activity and forward scattered protons, while exploring the role of pomeron-pomeron fusion and the identification of pseudoscalar mesons to elucidate the pomeron's spin structure.
AI.motivation: To explore central exclusive diffractive production and its mechanisms at hadron colliders, particularly under the context of LHC energies.
AI.method: Analysis involves the use of detectors to measure both midrapidity hadronic activity and the forward scattered protons, alongside a theoretical framework within the Regge approach to characterize the pomeron and study pseudoscalar meson identification.
AI.result: The study finds that central diffractive production is indeed dominated by pomeron-pomeron fusion, and provides insights into potential methods for identifying pseudoscalar mesons to clarify the spin structure of the pomeron.
AI.conclusion: Identifying specific mesons could significantly enhance the understanding of the pomeron's spin structure and contribute to the broader knowledge of diffractive processes in high-energy proton-proton collisions.

title: Predictive drift compensation of multi-frame STEM via live scan modification
summary: Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) is widely used tool for materials characterisation. However, being a scanned technique, STEM is susceptible to sample, stage or beam drift, manifesting as distortions within images or movement in the field-of-view during multi-frame imaging. Often this is corrected post-acquisition using image registration of multiple frames, but drift reduces the usable area common to all frames. Here we present a method to mitigate sample drift by analysing past frames to predict the sampling-grid points for the immediately future frame. We present this correction across two time-scales and two lengthscales. By offsetting the scan-grid framewise we remove long-range drift, and offsetting pixelwise we minimise intra-image warping. Examples are presented for both atomic-resolution imaging and lower-magnification in-situ video capture. The framework is general to raster, serpentine, interlaced and other scan patterns, as well as sequential or scan-rotation series STEM.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method for mitigating drift in scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) by predicting future sampling points based on past frames, improving image quality across various imaging scales and types.
AI.motivation: STEM imaging is prone to drift, leading to distortions and reduced usable areas, affecting image quality and analysis.
AI.method: The authors propose a predictive method to continually adjust the sampling grid based on previous frames, accommodating both long-range drift and intra-image warping.
AI.result: The method effectively corrects drift in STEM images of both atomic-resolution and lower-magnification in-situ video, showcasing its versatility across different imaging situations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enhances imaging accuracy in STEM by correcting drift dynamically, applicable to various scanning patterns and resolutions.

title: Science from the In Situ Exploration of the Proxima Centauri System
summary: In the future interstellar exploration at near-relativistic speeds will be possible using beamed energy laser propulsion. With this, spacecraft as small as gm mass picospacecraft become candidates for the exploration of deep space, with a trade space of velocity and mission duration versus mass. Here, we examine the potential science return from interstellar expeditions with Coracle laser-sail picospacecraft swarms and show how even with fast flybys at near relativistic velocities, a picospacecraft swarm could deliver gigapixel resolution of the target exoplanets. Our mission target is the planet Proxima b in the habitable zone (HZ) of the red dwarf Proxima Centauri, the tertiary (and nearest) component of the nearest star system, α Centauri. We explore science returns from such an expedition, both en route to Proxima and at the Proxima system, and conclude that initial small spacecraft expeditions would provide a substantial science return, including the ability to detect surface biology or a technological civilization, should either or both be established on the target planet.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the potential of picospacecraft swarms for interstellar exploration using laser propulsion, particularly targeting the exoplanet Proxima b to assess science returns.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to enable deep-space exploration at near-relativistic speeds with small spacecraft, enhancing our ability to study exoplanets.
AI.method: The study examines Coracle laser-sail picospacecraft swarms, focusing on mission designs that balance velocity, mass, and mission duration to optimize science returns.
AI.result: The findings indicate that even fast flybys can yield gigapixel-resolution imagery of target exoplanets, with significant potential for scientific discovery.
AI.conclusion: Initial missions with small spacecraft could lead to major discoveries regarding surface biology or technological civilizations on Proxima b, demonstrating the feasibility and benefits of such explorations.

title: Radio detection of supernova remnant G310.7-5.4 with $γ$-ray counterpart: Abeona SNR
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted in A&A
summary: G310.7-5.4 is a supernova remnant (SNR) candidate identified as a faint shell in the second epoch Molonglo Galactic Plane Survey (MGPS-2), but this has not been followed up with multi-wavelength observations until now. It is an example of an SNR at high Galactic latitude showing spatially coinciding $γ$-ray emission. Here, we make the first detailed investigation of the radio emission from the G310.7-5.4 region, aiming to characterise the radio structure, polarisation measurements and the coinciding GeV emission. We used recent radio continuum observations at 943.5 MHz from the EMU and the POSSUM surveys with ASKAP, as well as 16.5 years of Fermi-LAT observations. We furthermore considered the multiwavelength context of the object by investigating observations previously conducted with other instruments, such as infrared and X-ray surveys. We confirm the SNR candidate as a new supernova remnant, dubbed Abeona. We detect the presence of a faint, extended, bilateral radio shell of the size of around 30' diameter and ASKAP radio flux density of $1.5^{+1.5}_{-0.1}$ Jy with no obvious infrared counterparts. With a radio surface brightness of about $2.4^{+2.4}_{-0.1}\times10^{-22}$ W m$^{-2}$ Hz$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$, this SNR is one of the faintest radio SNRs known. The northern part of the shell shows linearly polarised radio emission, characteristic of synchrotron emission in SNRs. The physical size of the SNR is estimated to be around $42^{+42}_{-21}$ pc, which would give a distance of around $4.9^{+4.9}_{-2.5}$ kpc. Furthermore, the spatially coincident $γ$-ray source 4FGL J1413.9-6705 shows an energy flux of $1.26\pm0.35\times 10^{-6}$ MeV cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ with a significance of 5.7 $σ$ between 100 MeV and 100 GeV. The SNR is also put in context with known high-latitude SNRs with $γ$-ray counterparts and compared with their observational properties.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the radio properties of the supernova remnant (SNR) candidate G310.7-5.4, confirming it as a new SNR named Abeona, and detailing its faint radio emission and coinciding $	ext{γ}$-ray detection.
AI.motivation: To characterize the radio emission and properties of the previously unobserved SNR candidate G310.7-5.4, particularly given its high Galactic latitude and coinciding $	ext{γ}$-ray emission.
AI.method: Utilized radio continuum observations from the EMU and POSSUM surveys at 943.5 MHz and 16.5 years of Fermi-LAT data; also integrated previous multiwavelength observations, including infrared and X-ray surveys.
AI.result: Confirmed G310.7-5.4 as the new supernova remnant Abeona, detecting a faint, extended radio shell with a diameter of about 30' and a radio flux density of approximately $1.5^{+1.5}_{-0.1}$ Jy; identified linearly polarized emission consistent with synchrotron processes.
AI.conclusion: Brought G310.7-5.4 into the context of high-latitude SNRs and their $	ext{γ}$-ray emissions, contributing to the knowledge of faint SNRs in the Galaxy.

title: Introduction to transverse momentum imaging
comment: Submitted to a special issue of Particles collecting the NJU school's lecture notes
summary: This set of notes complements the lectures and recitation sessions discussed in the following graduate schools: HUGS at Jefferson Lab (years 2018, 2019, 2021), the International School and Workshop on Probing Hadron Structure at the Electron-Ion Collider at ICTS (2024), Frontiers in Nuclear and Hadronic Physics at GGI (2025), and the International Workshop and School on Hadron Structure and Strong Interactions at Nanjing University (2025).

AI.tldr: The notes complement various lectures and workshops in hadron structure and physics across multiple institutions from 2018 to 2025.
AI.motivation: To provide supplementary materials for graduate-level discussions on hadron structure and related topics.
AI.method: Compilation of lecture notes and discussions from multiple workshops and schools focused on hadron physics.
AI.result: The notes serve as educational support for graduate students attending these events.
AI.conclusion: These notes are intended to enhance understanding of hadron structure in the context of upcoming research initiatives.

title: Using Graph Neural Networks for hadronic clustering and to reduce beam background in the Belle~II electromagnetic calorimeter
summary: The Belle~II electromagnetic calorimeter consists of 8376 CsI(Tl) scintillation crystals and is not only used for measuring electromagnetic particles but also for identifying and determining the position of hadrons, particularly neutral\textbf{} hadrons. Recent data-taking periods have presented challenges for the current clustering method: Firstly, the record-breaking luminosities achieved by the SuperKEKB accelerator have increased background rates, leading to a higher number of crystals with energy depositions, and an overall increase in the total energy measured in the calorimeter. This resulted in poorer photon energy resolution and the reconstruction of more fake photon clusters. Secondly, challenges arise from the nature of hadronic interactions. In contrast to $γ$ and $e^{\pm}$, hadrons interacting in the calorimeter result in irregular, sometimes even disconnected energy depositions. These clusters can be misinterpreted as photon clusters, thereby reducing the position resolution of neutral hadrons or causing a complete misidentification of the hadron. Graph neural networks offer a promising solution to both challenges. By representing only crystals with an energy measurement as nodes, graphs capture the sparsity of the input. Using message-passing layers that learn the graph edges also helps to address the asymmetric sensor layout of Belle~II's ECL. In these proceedings, we will present a novel approach to identify the challenges in the detector simulation. Using this information, we train a Graph Neural Network to identify and remove unwanted depositions abefore clustering.

AI.tldr: The study proposes a Graph Neural Network (GNN) approach to enhance the identification and clustering of energy depositions in the Belle II electromagnetic calorimeter, addressing challenges from increased background noise and irregular hadronic interactions.
AI.motivation: Recent data-taking at Belle~II faced issues due to record luminosities and irregular hadronic particle interactions, leading to poor photon energy resolution and misidentification of neutral hadrons.
AI.method: The novel method utilizes Graph Neural Networks by representing energy depositions as nodes in a graph, employing message-passing layers to manage input sparsity and the detector's asymmetric layout.
AI.result: The approach aims to improve the photon energy resolution and accurately identify and cluster hadronic events, reducing fake clusters and misidentifications.
AI.conclusion: The implementation of GNNs shows potential in effectively managing the complexities of the Belle II detector simulation, leading to enhanced data analysis capabilities.

title: Quantum $f$-divergences via Nussbaum-Szkoła Distributions in Semifinite von Neumann Algebras
summary: In this article, we prove that the quantum $f$-divergence between two normal states on a semifinite von~Neumann algebra is equal to the classical $f$-divergence between two corresponding classical states, which are called Nussbaum-Szkoła distributions. This result has been proved by the second named author and T.C.~John for normal states on the von~Neumann algebra $\mathbb{B}(\mathscr{H})$ of all bounded operators on a Hilbert space $\mathscr{H}$. We extend their result for normal states on any semifinite von~Neumann algebra, not only $\mathbb{B}(\mathscr{H})$.

AI.tldr: The paper extends a previously established result connecting quantum and classical $f$-divergences from a specific case to all semifinite von Neumann algebras.
AI.motivation: To explore the relationship between quantum and classical $f$-divergences across a broader class of mathematical structures, promoting a deeper understanding of their connections.
AI.method: The authors build on existing work for normal states in a bounded operator setting and generalize these findings to any semifinite von Neumann algebra.
AI.result: The quantum $f$-divergence is shown to equal the classical $f$-divergence for normal states on any semifinite von Neumann algebra, identifying the classical counterparts as Nussbaum-Szkoła distributions.
AI.conclusion: The extension of this result supports a broader application of quantum-classical equivalences in information theory and statistical mechanics.

title: A 260-Liter Test Stand for Liquid Argon R&D
summary: We describe the design and performance of a 260-liter liquid argon (LAr) cryogenic test stand for liquid argon detector research and development at BNL. The system uses gas-phase argon purification with continuous pump-free circulation, in which boil-off argon gas is purified, recondensed, and returned to the cryostat by gravity without a mechanical recirculation pump; it also incorporates an upgraded condenser that increases the effective thermal contact area by a factor of 13 relative to the previously developed 20-liter system reported perviously. A liquid argon purity monitor is installed to measure the electron lifetime directly in LAr, enabling quantitative characterization of charge attenuation due to electronegative impurities. Under the operating conditions reported here, the demonstrated electron lifetime is 0.5 ms. The system is designed to enable rapid iteration of detector components in complete operational cycles, including pump-down, leak verification, cryogenic fill, stable operation, and warm-up, which can be completed within 7 days. Such a fast turnaround time, together with the medium-scale liquid volume and direct purity diagnostics, makes the facility well suited for testing and refining detector designs in support of large liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC) experiments.

AI.tldr: A new 260-liter liquid argon cryogenic test stand designed for efficient detector R&D at BNL features gas-phase argon purification and enhanced thermal contact area, enabling quick iteration and measurement of liquid argon purity.
AI.motivation: To advance research and development in liquid argon detectors, specifically for LArTPC experiments, by providing a reliable and efficient test facility.
AI.method: The system uses pump-free gas-phase argon purification with gravitational recirculation, an upgraded condenser for better thermal contact, and a purity monitor for measuring electron lifetime in LAr.
AI.result: The setup demonstrates an electron lifetime of 0.5 ms under reported operating conditions, and allows for rapid operational cycles (7 days) for detector component iterations.
AI.conclusion: This facility effectively supports the testing and refinement of liquid argon detector designs, making it advantageous for large-scale LArTPC experiments.

title: Photometric Super-Resolution for Improving Galaxy Morphological Measurements using Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks
comment: 28 pages, 18 figures. Submitted to AAS Journals on March 13, 2026
summary: The measurement of galaxy morphological parameters from astronomical images features in a wide range of modern analyses, including galaxy evolution and cosmological weak lensing studies. The precision and accuracy of morphological parameter estimation can be influenced by several key factors. The effective seeing of the image, summarized by the point spread function (PSF), limits how galaxy features or light profiles are resolved. The pixel scale of the detector also influences the resolution and the amount of statistical information available for a given object. The depth of the observations determines the signal-to-noise ratio of the image. Improving each of these factors is very costly, either in terms of detector upgrades, observatory design, or observing time. Here, we develop a conditional generative adversarial network, called Neo, trained to transform existing ground-based images into sharper, finer-scale images comparable to space-based image quality. We demonstrate that Neo improves the accuracy of measured morphological parameters by factors of $2$-$10$ when trained to translate Subaru Hyper Suprime-Camera (HSC) images to approximate Hubble Space Telescope (HST) data. Neo is designed for applicability to ongoing, large-scale surveys such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) conducted by Vera C. Rubin Observatory in combination with space telescopes such as HST, James Webb Space Telescope, and Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. These results suggest that Neo could be used to improve both cosmological and galaxy evolution analyses based on massive, ground-based survey datasets like LSST. The model code is open source and available at https://purl.archive.org/neo/code.

AI.tldr: The study introduces Neo, a conditional generative adversarial network that enhances galaxy imaging by transforming ground-based images to mimick space-based quality, significantly improving morphological parameter estimation.
AI.motivation: To enhance the precision and accuracy of galaxy morphological parameter measurements which are crucial in studies of galaxy evolution and cosmological weak lensing, given the limitations of ground-based telescopes.
AI.method: Developed a conditional generative adversarial network (Neo) to convert ground-based Subaru HSC images into higher quality, space-based equivalent images, improving resolution and detail.
AI.result: Neo achieved a 2-10 fold improvement in accuracy of morphological parameters when translating Subaru HSC images to match HST data.
AI.conclusion: Neo is a valuable tool for improving analyses of large-scale astronomical surveys and is open-source for community use.

title: Search for Anisotropic Pair Halos Associated with Blazar Jets
summary:
The origin of intergalactic magnetic fields (IGMFs) remains one of the key open questions in cosmology. Gamma-ray pair halos produced by electromagnetic cascades from TeV-emitting blazars provide a powerful indirect probe of these fields. In this work, we present a novel search for pair halos that explicitly exploits their expected anisotropic morphology, aligning with the projected orientation of blazar jets on the sky. Using a Monte Carlo framework to model the spatial distribution of cascade emission, we identify an optimal sample of 21 high-synchrotron-peaked BL Lac objects with well-constrained jet position angles from radio interferometry. By rotating and stacking \textit{Fermi}-LAT observations of these sources along their jet directions, we enhance sensitivity to anisotropic extended emission that would be diluted in traditional orientation-agnostic analyses.
  Applying a likelihood analysis to the combined dataset, we find evidence for a non-zero IGMF, excluding the null hypothesis at $3.8σ$ level and obtaining a best-fit field strength of $B_0 = 2.8 \times 10^{-16}\,\mathrm{G}$, with a $99\%$ confidence interval of $0.9 \times 10^{-16}\,\mathrm{G} < B_0 < 8.9 \times 10^{-16}\,\mathrm{G}$. Our result is consistent with previous constraints from spectral, spatial, and temporal studies, while demonstrating that incorporating anisotropic information provides a significant gain in sensitivity. This approach opens a new avenue for probing intergalactic magnetism and highlights the potential of future high-angular-resolution gamma-ray observations to directly image pair halos and map magnetic fields in cosmic voids.

AI.tldr: The study investigates intergalactic magnetic fields (IGMFs) using gamma-ray pair halos from blazars, applying a novel anisotropic analysis method that enhances sensitivity and finds significant evidence for a non-zero IGMF.
AI.motivation: Understanding the origin of intergalactic magnetic fields is crucial in cosmology, and gamma-ray pair halos from blazars provide a unique method to probe these fields.
AI.method: The study utilized a Monte Carlo framework to model the spatial distribution of cascade emissions from 21 high-synchrotron-peaked BL Lac objects, rotating and stacking Fermi-LAT observations along jet directions to enhance sensitivity to anisotropic emission.
AI.result: The analysis revealed evidence for a non-zero IGMF, with a best-fit field strength of $B_0 = 2.8 \times 10^{-16}\mathrm{G}$, excluding the null hypothesis at a $3.8σ$ level.
AI.conclusion: This approach significantly increases sensitivity to intergalactic magnetism and suggests potential for future observations to directly image pair halos and map magnetic fields.

title: Photon and neutrino fluxes from spheroidal dwarf galaxies in a decaying DM model
summary: In this work, we investigate a decaying dark matter scenario and its associated indirect detection signatures. The model consists of a scalar singlet with a lifetime exceeding the age of the Universe. Stability is ensured by a $Z_2$ symmetry imposed on the Lagrangian, allowing decay through a non-minimal gravitational coupling. The decay of dark matter produces Standard Model particles, which subsequently yield products such as gamma rays, neutrinos, and charged particles. We computed the gamma-ray and neutrino fluxes generated by this candidate in the Milky Way and in 14 dwarf spheroidal galaxies, as well as the corresponding expected number of events in selected experiments, using dedicated numerical tools. Results are presented for three benchmark masses and three coupling values consistent with cosmological constraints, showing that the predicted signals can be observable in specific regions of parameter space.

AI.tldr: The paper explores a decaying dark matter model, analyzing its indirect detection signatures and potential observability in gamma rays and neutrinos.
AI.motivation: To understand the implications of a decaying dark matter scenario and its observable signatures in astrophysical contexts.
AI.method: The authors utilized numerical tools to compute gamma-ray and neutrino fluxes from a scalar singlet dark matter model, validating against cosmological constraints and analyzing multiple benchmark parameters.
AI.result: Predicted signals from the dark matter decay can be observed in particular regions of the parameter space, with computed event rates for Milky Way and dwarf galaxies.
AI.conclusion: The study indicates significant potential for observational evidence of decaying dark matter through specific experimental setups.

title: Toward designing workload-aware Surface Code Architectures
summary: Practical quantum advantage is expected to depend on fault-tolerant quantum computing, although the architectural overhead needed to support fault tolerance is still extremely high. Prior FTQC designs generally emphasize either fast logical-qubit accessibility at the cost of significant qubit overhead, or high logical-qubit density at the cost of added workload latency. We propose an architecture that balances these competing objectives by placing surface-code patches around an ancilla-centric region, which yields nearly uniform ancilla access for all data qubits. Building on this design, we introduce a new workload-driven placement method that uses the $T$-gate profile of an application to determine an effective floorplan. We further provide a reconfigurable optimization for reducing the latency of $Y$-gate measurements on a per-workload basis. To improve flexibility, we also study concurrent execution of multiple programs on the same architecture. Numerical evaluation indicates that our approach keeps cycles per instruction near the optimal regime while reducing the number of required data tiles by up to $\sim21\%$, and achieves up to $\sim90\%$ efficiency when running 10 programs concurrently.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a balanced architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) that optimizes logical qubit accessibility while reducing qubit overhead and latency. It introduces a workload-driven placement method and enhances the flexibility of concurrent program execution, achieving significant efficiency gains in resource usage.
AI.motivation: To address the high architectural overhead and latency in fault-tolerant quantum computing, balancing fast logical-qubit accessibility with qubit density.
AI.method: Proposes an architecture with surface-code patches around an ancilla-centric region, introducing a workload-driven placement method based on $T$-gate profiles, and implements reconfigurable optimizations for $Y$-gate measurement latency.
AI.result: Numerical evaluations show reduced cycles per instruction to near-optimal levels and a reduction in required data tiles by $	ext{~21	ext{%}}$, achieving up to $	ext{~90	ext{%}}$ efficiency with concurrent execution of 10 programs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture significantly enhances resource efficiency in fault-tolerant quantum computing while supporting multiple program executions.

title: Measuring Tianlai's primary beam using sky model
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures, Accepted by Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: We present the beam pattern measurement of the Tianlai Cylinder Pathfinder Array. As it is a pure drift-scan instrument, we exploit the North-South motion of the Sun to demonstrate that the primary beam is factorizable. Leveraging this property, we decompose the primary beam into independent East-West (E-W) and North-South (N-S) components. Using the Sun as a calibration source, we obtain the E-W beam profiles at various elevations, applying normalization to eliminate the effects of solar activity. Subsequently, we simulate the observed signals using a sky map model to derive the best-fit N-S beam. The results of this work are consistent with previous expectations.

AI.tldr: This study measures the beam pattern of the Tianlai Cylinder Pathfinder Array using the Sun as a calibration source, leading to independent E-W and N-S beam decomposition.
AI.motivation: To accurately characterize the beam pattern of a drift-scan telescope, leveraging the unique motion of the Sun and the factorizability of the primary beam.
AI.method: The study uses the Sun's motion to measure E-W beam profiles and simulates signals with a sky map to derive N-S beam profiles, applying normalization for solar activity effects.
AI.result: The E-W and N-S beam profiles were successfully extracted and found to conform to prior expectations, confirming the measurement method's validity.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the feasibility of using the Sun for beam pattern calibration and decomposition in drift-scan instruments.

title: Graph-theoretic determination of massless modes in latticized theory-space models
comment: 13 pages, 2 captioned figures; Includes a Mathematica notebook in the ancillary directory implementing the Dulmage-Mendelsohn decomposition for bipartite graphs
summary: A graph-theoretic method is introduced for analyzing fermion mass spectra in latticized theory-space models, including chain models arising from dimensional deconstruction. Fermion mass terms are mapped to bipartite graphs, with fields as vertices and nonvanishing mass terms as edges. The number of massless modes is shown to be fixed by the cardinality of a maximum matching of the associated graph. Moreover, the wave-function support of these modes is restricted to fields reachable from exposed or unmatched vertices by even-length maximum-matching-alternating paths, as characterized by the Dulmage-Mendelsohn decomposition. These results depend only on the topology of latticized theory space and are independent of model parameters. The method enables a systematic construction of latticized models with prescribed numbers and localization properties of massless modes.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a graph-theoretic technique to analyze fermion mass spectra in latticized theory-space models, establishing how massless modes correlate to graph theory concepts.
AI.motivation: To provide a systematic framework for analyzing fermion masses in complex models, addressing the limitations of existing methods in capturing localization properties.
AI.method: Mass terms are represented as edges in bipartite graphs; the number of massless modes is determined using maximum matching, with paths defined by graph decomposition techniques.
AI.result: The study reveals that the number of massless modes corresponds to the maximum matching in a bipartite graph, and their wave-function support is limited to specific graph paths.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method is robust, reliant solely on the topology of the theory space, allowing for structured construction of models with tailored localization characteristics.

title: Bootstrapping Open Quantum Many-body Systems with Absorbing Phase Transitions
summary: We demonstrate that combining the positivity of density matrices with steady-state conditions yields a systematic bootstrap method for studying open quantum many-body systems governed by Lindblad master equations on infinite lattices, which exhibit absorbing phase transitions. As a concrete example, we apply this method to the quantum contact process with an absorbing state. We obtain bootstrap bounds on steady-state expectation values, the critical coupling, certain ratios of expectation values in the nontrivial steady state in the supercritical phase, and the Liouvillian spectral gap in the subcritical phase.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a bootstrap method utilizing positivity of density matrices for analyzing open quantum systems with absorbing phase transitions, specifically applied to the quantum contact process.
AI.motivation: The study tackles the challenge of analyzing open quantum many-body systems that follow Lindblad dynamics and exhibit phase transitions, which are crucial for understanding quantum behavior in these systems.
AI.method: The authors combine the positivity of density matrices with steady-state conditions to develop a systematic bootstrap method tailored for infinite lattice quantum systems governed by Lindblad master equations.
AI.result: The method yields bounds on various steady-state properties, including critical coupling parameters and the Liouvillian spectral gap, enhancing the understanding of nontrivial steady states and phase transitions.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides valuable insights into the behavior of open quantum many-body systems at critical points, showcasing its applicability to specific models like the quantum contact process.

title: Valley-Aware Optimal Control of Spin Shuttling Using Cryogenic Integrated Electronics
comment: 16 pages, 11 figures (3 PNGs, 7 PDFs and 1 diagram made with tikzpicture in TEX), The paper will be submitted to the journal Quantum Science and Technologies
summary: Electron shuttling is emerging as a key mechanism for enabling long-range coupling in scalable spin-qubit architectures. Bringing shuttling waveform generation into the cryostat can improve scalability, but imposes strict area and power constraints on the control electronics. Concurrently, shuttling in Si/SiGe is further limited by a spatially varying valley splitting that induces spin--valley mixing and degrades coherence. Here, we make three contributions that address these limitations jointly: (i) an end-to-end co-simulation framework that combines disorder-informed valley maps with transistor-level cryogenic circuit simulations including electronic noise; (ii) a fully integrated cryogenic shuttling-signal generator tailored to velocity modulation, enabling period-wise waveform shaping through discrete circuit settings stored in on-chip memory; and (iii) a noise-aware optimization procedure that tunes only these implementable circuit controls, using one of four discrete resistor settings per period, to generate high-fidelity shuttling sequences. Across simulated valley and noise realizations in our co-simulation framework, the optimized velocity-modulation waveforms improve transport performance, achieving an average shuttling fidelity of $99.99 \pm 0.007\%$ at $v_{\mathrm{avg}} = 20~\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ over a distance of $10~μ\mathrm{m}$, while maintaining active analog power consumption in the tens of $μ\mathrm{W}$ during shuttling. This validates on-chip storage and replay of optimized control settings as a practical strategy to mitigate valley disorder in scalable shuttling architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents advancements in electron shuttling for spin-qubit architectures by integrating simulation frameworks, tailored shuttling signal generators, and noise-aware optimization procedures, achieving high fidelity and low power consumption in shuttling operations.
AI.motivation: To improve the scalability of spin-qubit architectures through better electron shuttling methods while addressing valley splitting and noise issues.
AI.method: The authors developed a co-simulation framework, an integrated cryogenic shuttling-signal generator for waveform shaping, and a noise-aware optimization process to produce high-fidelity shuttling sequences.
AI.result: The optimized velocity-modulation waveforms boosted transport performance, yielding an average shuttling fidelity of 99.99% at an average speed of 20 m/s over a 10 μm distance, with minimal power consumption.
AI.conclusion: The findings validate the use of on-chip memory for storing optimized control settings as an effective approach to counteract valley disorder in scalable electron shuttling architectures.

title: Review: A new method for estimation and use of systematic errors in Poisson regression
comment: Accepted for Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences - Astrostatistics. This is a review of https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...980..139B and https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...980..140B presented at the sys2025 workshop in Huntsville, AL (Nov 14-17. 2025)
summary: A new method for including systematic errors in the regression with Poisson data is reviewed in this contribution, with emphasis on applications to astronomical spectra. The method consists of generalizing the usual Poisson log-likelihood, known as the Cash statistic $C_{min}$, and its associated likelihood-ratio statistic $ΔC$, to include the presence of systematic sources of uncertainty. Advantages of this new method include its modeling simplicity and its ability to assess both the level of systematics and the goodness of fit at the same time, including for a nested model component.

AI.tldr: A new method for incorporating systematic errors into Poisson regression is presented, enhancing the modeling of astronomical spectra.
AI.motivation: Addressing systematic uncertainties in Poisson data regression is crucial for accurate astronomical analysis.
AI.method: The method generalizes the Cash statistic $C_{min}$ and the likelihood-ratio statistic $ΔC$ to include systematic errors in the analysis.
AI.result: It simplifies the modeling process while assessing systematic uncertainties and fit quality simultaneously, including for nested models.
AI.conclusion: This new approach effectively combines simplicity with comprehensive error assessment, improving analytical accuracy in astronomical data.

title: Practical HPCQC Integration with QDMI: A Real-Hardware Case Study with IQM Systems
summary: Quantum computers are moving into HPC centers, and the main challenge is now integration rather than pure hardware access. Many current software paths still depend on vendor-specific adapter chains between user SDKs, schedulers, and backend APIs. This pattern makes operations more complex than necessary and slows the transition from pilots to production workflows. We present a practical integration path centered on the Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI). Using IQM superconducting systems as a hardware case study, we implement an IQM-backed QDMI layer and connect it to two software layers that HPC centers working with quantum computers already care about: Slurm-based job execution and Qiskit-facing user workflows. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/iqm-finland/QDMI-on-IQM. The key message is simple: integrating quantum hardware into HPC does not have to be a bespoke engineering effort for each backend. Once the software-hardware boundary is standardized, large parts of the stack become reusable across providers and deployment styles. Our results do not claim that standardization eliminates all HPCQC challenges. They show that this specific boundary can already be standardized today in a way that is practical for users, operators, and vendors.

AI.tldr: Integration is the primary challenge for quantum computing in HPC centers, addressed by the Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI).
AI.motivation: The shift from hardware access to integration complicates operations and hinders the transition to production workflows.
AI.method: Implementation of a QDMI layer using IQM superconducting systems, interfaced with Slurm and Qiskit.
AI.result: The integration demonstrates that standardization of the software-hardware boundary can greatly streamline processes across quantum computing providers.
AI.conclusion: Standardizing the boundary enhances usability and reusability, though not all challenges in HPCQC are eliminated.

title: A Python/CuPy Software Correlator for QUEST: Real-Time Performance and Initial Imaging
summary: We present a Python/CuPy FX software correlator for small radio interferometer arrays and evaluate it on QUEST (Qilu University Explorer Survey Telescope). The system combines multi-threaded data ingest, pinned-memory host-device transfers, GPU-accelerated correlation, Polyphase Filter Bank channelization, MAD-based RFI flagging, and delay/phase calibration in a single workflow aimed at array commissioning. On a single NVIDIA RTX 4090D GPU, the implementation reaches a peak throughput of 1.51 GB/s, which is sufficient for real-time operation in the four-antenna mode tested here. After calibration, the visibility phase across a clean 1.32-1.38 GHz band is flattened to a residual scatter of a few degrees. Using the calibrated visibilities, we form a four-antenna synthesis image of Cassiopeia A; the CLEANed image recovers a compact source at the phase center and reduces image-domain background fluctuations from order 0.1 to a few 0.01 Jy/beam. These results indicate that the software is suitable for small-array commissioning and initial synthesis imaging on QUEST. A GNSS-based beam measurement is included as a supporting commissioning check.

AI.tldr: Development of a Python/CuPy software correlator for small radio interferometers, successfully tested on the QUEST telescope with promising throughput and imaging results.
AI.motivation: To enhance real-time data processing and imaging capability for small radio interferometer arrays, specifically for the QUEST telescope.
AI.method: Employs multi-threaded data ingestion, GPU acceleration, and advanced techniques for calibration and RFI flagging in a streamlined workflow.
AI.result: Achieved a peak throughput of 1.51 GB/s on a NVIDIA RTX 4090D GPU, enabling effective real-time operation and producing a high-quality synthesis image of Cassiopeia A.
AI.conclusion: The software is effective for commissioning small arrays and initial imaging, demonstrating significant improvements in visibility calibration and background fluctuation reduction.

title: SN 2007it on the RISE -- a radio detection of an interacting supernova 18 years post-explosion
summary: We report the first detection of radio emission from the Type II supernova SN 2007it, located at a distance of 12.2 Mpc in NGC 5530. The observations were obtained with the Australian Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) more than 18 yr after the explosion as part of the Rebrightening in Interacting Supernova Emission (RISE) program, which monitors nearby core-collapse supernovae for late-time interaction with dense circumstellar material. SN 2007it was detected on 2026 April 8 (08:00-12:00 UTC) at 5.5 GHz with a flux density of $3.30 \pm 0.13$ mJy and at 9.0 GHz with $3.54 \pm 0.24$ mJy. Its non-detection in publicly available 0.88 GHz ASKAP data from 2026 January 11 suggests either rapidly rising emission or significant internal absorption at lower frequencies. We assess the prospects for detection at other wavelengths and encourage coordinated follow-up observations across the radio, optical, X-ray, and $γ$-ray band

AI.tldr: First detection of radio emission from supernova SN 2007it, 18 years after explosion, indicating potential interaction with circumstellar material.
AI.motivation: To monitor late-time interactions of core-collapse supernovae with dense circumstellar material and understand their emission mechanisms.
AI.method: Radio observations conducted with the Australian Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) at multiple frequencies post-explosion.
AI.result: Successful detection of radio emission at 5.5 GHz and 9.0 GHz, with significant flux densities, while non-detection at lower frequencies raises questions about internal absorption.
AI.conclusion: Encourages further multi-wavelength follow-up to investigate emission mechanisms and interactions.

title: Chiral first order phase transition at finite baryon density and zero temperature from self-consistent pole masses in the linear sigma model with quarks
summary: We use the two-flavor Linear Sigma Model with quarks as an effective description of QCD to investigate the nature of the chiral phase transition at finite baryon chemical potential and zero temperature. We work at one-loop order to set up and solve the system of self-consistent coupled equations for the particle pole masses. The chemical potential-dependent value of the chiral order parameter is obtained by minimizing the one-loop effective potential. This treatment goes beyond the conventional ring-diagram approximation and provides a description valid for arbitrary values of the chemical potential. We find that the phase transition is of first order, and occurs when the quark chemical potential reaches the value of the vacuum quark mass for the chosen set of parameters. The first order nature of the transition is signaled by the discontinuous behavior of the chiral condensate, the masses and the couplings. The thermodynamics of the system is readily implemented and in particular, we find that the square of the speed of sound exhibits a discontinuity at the phase transition and then smoothly approaches the conformal limit from below.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the chiral phase transition at finite baryon chemical potential using the two-flavor Linear Sigma Model with quarks, finding it to be first-order, characterized by discontinuities in various thermodynamic quantities.
AI.motivation: To explore the chiral phase transition in QCD at finite baryon chemical potential and zero temperature, extending beyond conventional approximations.
AI.method: Utilizing the two-flavor Linear Sigma Model, the study sets up self-consistent coupled equations at one-loop order to minimize the effective potential for the chiral order parameter.
AI.result: The phase transition is identified as first-order, triggered when the chemical potential equals the vacuum quark mass, indicated by discontinuities in the chiral condensate and other properties.
AI.conclusion: The speed of sound exhibits a discontinuous change at the phase transition and approaches the conformal limit smoothly thereafter.

title: Co-Designing Error Mitigation and Error Detection for Logical Qubits
summary:
Near-term quantum workloads demand error management, yet the two lightest-weight techniques, Quantum Error Detection (QED) and Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC), have complementary cost profiles whose joint architectural design space remains unexplored. QED encodes logical qubits and discards error-flagged runs, filtering noise with low qubit overhead but leaving residual errors; PEC can correct these in software, but at exponential cost in noise strength. If QED efficiently reduces per-gate noise, PEC's cost savings can outweigh QED's discard overhead; realizing this, however, requires solving two system-level design challenges.
  First, the \textit{QED interval} -- how often detection cycles are inserted -- is a tunable architectural parameter governing the cost-accuracy tradeoff. We derive an efficiency condition and show that the canonical one-cycle-per-gate frequency does not achieve break-even in any code we evaluate, while optimized intervals on high-rate Iceberg codes do. Second, we discover that naive PEC+QED integration \textit{degrades} accuracy below the QED-only baseline. The root cause is a transient error profile in the first detection cycle that corrupts PEC's noise model. We develop \textit{steady-state extraction}, a co-designed characterization protocol that isolates steady-state error behavior, reducing estimation bias by up to $10.2\times$. On a $[[6,4,2]]$ Iceberg code running QAOA ($p{=}4$--$8$) with a fixed shot budget, PEC+QED achieves $2$--$11\times$ lower absolute error and up to $31\times$ lower MSE versus PEC on physical qubits, with per-interval savings compounding over interval depth.

AI.tldr: The paper explores the joint architectural design of Quantum Error Detection (QED) and Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC) to improve error management in near-term quantum workloads, identifying design challenges and proposing optimizations that enhance efficiency and accuracy.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of current quantum error management techniques, and to explore their complementary nature for improved performance in near-term quantum computing.
AI.method: The authors derive an efficiency condition for the QED interval tuning, demonstrate that conventional single-cycle detection does not achieve optimal results, and develop a protocol called steady-state extraction to refine PEC's noise model.
AI.result: Optimized QED intervals on high-rate Iceberg codes showed significant error reduction, with PEC+QED achieving 2–11 times lower absolute error and up to 31 times lower mean squared error (MSE) compared to PEC alone on physical qubits.
AI.conclusion: Integrating QED and PEC effectively reduces errors in quantum workloads, but requires careful tuning of the detection cycle and attention to the integration process to avoid degradation of accuracy.

title: Detections of nearly bias-free core shifts with 5-30 $μ$as precisions at 8-43 GHz in BL Lacertae
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: When a radio jet is partially optically thick in the launching region, its apparent compact core may display frequency-dependent positional shifts. High-precision astrometric measurements of core shifts enable astronomers to pinpoint the jet's origin and place tight constraints on the magnetic field. BL Lacertae, the archetypal BL Lac object, hosts a highly variable and well-collimated jet. To independently constrain its innermost core shifts, we conducted very long baseline interferometric (VLBI) observations at 8.4, 12.4, 15.2, 23.6, and 43.2 GHz. By exploiting a nearby (13.3 arcmin) steep-spectrum calibrator (NVSS J220340+420839) through inverse phase-referencing VLBI astrometry, we detect nearly unbiased two-dimensional core shift measurements with state-of-the-art precisions of 5-30 $μ$as, which are significant at $>3σ$ confidence. The core shift between 8.4 and 43.2 GHz reaches 250 $μ$as. The apparent core shifts scale with frequency as $ν^{-1/k_r}$, implying the existence of an optically thick region in the upstream of jet. The derived core-shift index, $k_r\!=\!1.18^{+0.59}_{-0.34}$, is consistent, within uncertainties, with the canonical $k_r\!=\!1$ expected under energy equipartition between the jet particle and magnetic field energy densities, while allowing for modest deviations given that BL Lacertae was captured in a flaring state.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes frequency-dependent core shifts in the radio jet of BL Lacertae using VLBI observations to constrain magnetic field properties.
AI.motivation: Understanding core shifts in radio jets aids in identifying their origin and magnetic field constraints.
AI.method: Very long baseline interferometric (VLBI) observations were conducted at multiple GHz frequencies, utilizing phase-referencing techniques for precision astrometry.
AI.result: Significant core shift measurements were achieved, with a maximum shift of 250 μas between 8.4 and 43.2 GHz, revealing a scaling relationship with frequency.
AI.conclusion: The derived core-shift index suggests the presence of an optically thick region, consistent with energy equipartition, while accommodating flaring state deviations.

title: Target-Mass Corrections in the OPE Sum-Rule Approach to Quarkonium-Nucleon Interactions with Global-Fit PDFs: an $x$-Resolved Analysis
summary: We revisit the operator-product-expansion sum-rule approach to inelastic quarkonium-nucleon interactions using global-fit parton distribution functions ABMP16, MSHT20, CT18 and NNPDF4.0. In contrast to the original analyses, our goal is not limited to updating the PDF input, but is to resolve the full chain from the gluon distribution $g(x,Q)$ to the Mellin moments $A_n(Q)$, the corresponding sum rules, and the resulting cross section $σ_{ΦN}(s)$. We perform an $x$-resolved analysis of the TMC effect by studying the weighted moment densities entering the sum rules and their decomposition into different $x$-regions. This allows us to determine which parts of the gluon distribution dominate individual Mellin moments and how the finite target mass suppresses their contributions. We show that the magnitude of the TMC effect is controlled not only by the universal kinematic weight appearing in the modified sum rules, but also by the way in which a given global-fit PDF redistributes the support of the moments between the small-, intermediate- and large-$x$ regions. The resulting framework provides a transparent reanalysis of quarkonium-nucleon sum rules and clarifies the role of current PDF information in predictions for $σ_{ΦN}(s)$.

AI.tldr: This paper updates the operator-product-expansion sum-rule approach for inelastic quarkonium-nucleon interactions, analyzing gluon distributions and their effects on cross section calculations using modern parton distribution functions.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to enhance the understanding of quarkonium-nucleon interactions by improving the analysis of parton distribution functions (PDFs) and their impact on the resulting cross sections.
AI.method: The authors utilize global-fit PDFs to conduct an $x$-resolved analysis of the target mass corrections (TMC) effect, examining how contributions from different gluon distribution regions influence Mellin moments and sum rules.
AI.result: The study reveals that the TMC effect's magnitude is affected by both the kinematic weight in modified sum rules and the redistribution of support across small-, intermediate-, and large-$x$ regions by different global-fit PDFs.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a clearer framework for analyzing quarkonium-nucleon sum rules and emphasizes the significance of current PDF information in predictive models for cross sections.

title: Technically Natural Suppression of Fifth Force
summary: Light scalars generically mediate a fifth force incompatible with local tests of gravity unless their couplings are parametrically suppressed or screening mechanisms are introduced. We demonstrate that such suppression can arise from symmetry. We propose a $Z_2$-symmetric mirror extension of the Standard Model within a bi-conformal gravity construction, where spontaneous breaking of scale invariance produces a light scalaron as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson. This scalaron couples to the difference of trace anomalies between the Standard Model and mirror sectors. We find a parameter-independent correlation between the fifth-force strength $α$ and the scalaron mass $m_σ$, with the proportionality set by QCD observables and the electroweak scale. The Standard Model predicts $α\sim 10^{-4}$ at meter scales for $m_σ\sim 10^{-7}$ eV, which is directly in the target window of next-generation experiments. In contrast to environmental screening mechanisms, this suppression mechanism follows directly from symmetry rather than nonlinear scalar dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a $Z_2$-symmetric mirror extension of the Standard Model to explain the suppression of a fifth force mediated by light scalars, using symmetry principles instead of traditional screening methods.
AI.motivation: To address the incompatibility of light scalars with local gravity tests, proposing a model that avoids issues with fifth force detection.
AI.method: Introducing a $Z_2$-symmetric mirror extension of the Standard Model combined with bi-conformal gravity, leading to a light scalaron arising from spontaneous scale invariance breaking.
AI.result: Establishes a parameter-independent relationship between fifth-force strength and scalaron mass, with numerical predictions aligning with next-generation experimental targets.
AI.conclusion: The suppression of the fifth force derived from symmetry principles offers an alternative to nonlinear dynamics, potentially facilitating the search for light scalars in future experiments.

title: Measurement and feedback-driven adaptive dynamics in the classical and quantum kicked top
summary: In classical dynamical systems, stochastic feedback can stabilize otherwise unstable periodic orbits, giving rise to distinct controlled and uncontrolled phases as the rate of control application is varied.
